text.name: Samarkand
text.summary: Samarkand is the regional capital: 600,000-plus residents, 215 mahallas, major universities, an international airport and high-speed rail. In 2026 its territory was enlarged almost 2.5-fold.

p: Samarkand sits in the Zarafshan valley, on the left bank of the river, about 700 metres above sea level. It is the capital of Samarkand Region and the seat of its government. Its historic core has been on UNESCO’s World Heritage List since 2001 as “Samarkand – Crossroads of Cultures”, yet this is no open-air museum: hundreds of thousands of people live, study and work here.

The climate is dry and continental, with hot, almost rainless summers and short, fickle winters. On 1991–2020 normals, January averages +2.3 °C and July +27.2 °C; annual precipitation is around 380 mm, most of it falling in late winter and spring. The most pleasant months for a visit are April–May and September–October.

body.h: How the city is laid out
p: Samarkand currently has no districts: the city is made up of 215 mahalla (neighbourhood) assemblies and also includes the settlements of Kimyogarlar, Farhod and Khishrav. The east is the old city of narrow lanes and courtyard houses around the Registan, Bibi-Khanym and Siyob Bazaar. After 1868 a planned “new town” of broad boulevards grew up to the west, and University Boulevard with its Imperial-era buildings still defines the centre. To the north rise the mounds of ancient Afrasiyab; Soviet-era housing blocks spread the city further.

On the eastern edge, the Silk Road Samarkand complex (2022) groups hotels, a congress hall and the Eternal City (Boqiy Shahar), a stylised old town. A new chapter began on 8 August 2026, when Uzbekistan’s Senate approved abolishing Samarkand District and transferring 17,226.5 hectares to the city. Samarkand’s territory will grow from about 11,800 to nearly 29,000 hectares, and its population is projected to approach 880,000. The reform is very recent, so the population and area figures below are pre-expansion.

According to official statistics, Samarkand had 605,800 permanent residents on 1 January 2026 (551,700 in 2021). The city has always been multi-ethnic: alongside Uzbeks and Tajiks live Russians, Armenians, Tatars, Koreans, Iranians and others. Uzbek is the state language, but Tajik and Russian are heard just as often, and many Samarkandis switch easily between them.
Samarkand Region is the country’s most populous: the 2026 census counted over 4.4 million people (preliminary results).

Samarkand State University, named after Sharof Rashidov, traces its roots to a Higher Pedagogical Institute founded in 1927; the State Medical University dates from 1930. Others include institutes of foreign languages and of architecture and civil engineering, and the Silk Road International University of Tourism and Cultural Heritage. The Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Archaeology, based here, leads research on Afrasiyab and the Zarafshan valley.

The city is the backbone of the regional economy. It leads the region in industrial output per head and accounts for over a quarter (26.2%) of regional market services. Major employers include the SamAvto bus and truck plant and chemical, food, wine and textile factories; silk-carpet weaving, embroidery and ceramics live on in workshops open to visitors.

Tourism is growing fastest. Samarkand hosted the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in September 2022, the 43rd session of the UNESCO General Conference in October–November 2025 and the 46th Chess Olympiad in September 2026. Since 1997 the Registan has staged the biennial Sharq Taronalari international music festival.

The international airport, 6 km north of the centre, is the country’s second-largest. Afrosiyob high-speed trains reach Tashkent in about two hours and Bukhara in roughly ninety minutes; trains to Khiva and international services also call here. By road, the M39 runs to Tashkent and Termez and the M37 to Bukhara; the Tajik border is about 35 km away.

In town there are modern trams (two lines since 2017), buses and cheap taxis. In August 2026 more than 250 buses served 23 routes, with the fleet due to reach 500; city buses may now run up to 12 km beyond the city limits.

The city began on the Afrasiyab plateau to the north; archaeologists date its origins to the 8th–7th centuries BC, though the exact date is debated. Classical writers called it Marakanda, which Alexander the Great took in 329 BC. As the capital of Sogdiana it was one of the richest stops on the Silk Road; the Arabs arrived in 712, followed by the Samanids and Karakhanids. Genghis Khan’s army sacked the city in 1220, and from 1370 Samarkand was the capital of Amir Timur’s empire: Gur-e-Amir, Bibi-Khanym, Shah-i-Zinda and Ulugh Beg’s observatory belong to that age, while the Registan ensemble took shape between the 15th and 17th centuries.

From the 16th to the 19th century the city belonged to the Khanate, later Emirate, of Bukhara. Russian troops took it in 1868, and the Trans-Caspian Railway arrived in 1888. From 1925 to 1930 Samarkand was the capital of the Uzbek SSR. Since independence its monuments have been restored; in 2007 the city marked its 2,750th anniversary. The full story is in the History section.
